food.text: The 16th-century Flemish herbalist and diplomat Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq described Ottoman culinary culture as "very frugal". In his account, a simple meal of bread and salt, garlic or onion and yoghurt was all that was needed for nourishment.

Ottoman trade introduced new ingredients to the regional cuisines of the empire, which included the Balkans. Fernand Braudel credits the Ottomans with introducing rice, sesame and maize to the region.

Cornmeal, known as polenta or mămăligă, became a major part of the cuisines of the Balkans, as well as those of Poland, Italy and the Caucasus. Maize is much less common in most European diets than it is in the Americas, which makes this Balkan staple stand out.

Thessaloniki has been home to a Sephardic Jewish community since the late 15th century, following its expulsion from Spain in 1492. The community brought a culinary tradition that blended Spanish, North African, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean influences.

The monastic community of Mount Athos has its own distinctive traditional cuisine, built on bread, olive oil, wine, olives and vegetables. Mount Athos is also described as the oldest vineyard and site of viticulture in Greece, going back more than a thousand years.

art.text: Mainland Greece stayed under Ottoman rule for four centuries, so it took no part in the Renaissance and the artistic movements that followed in Western Europe. Islands such as Crete and the Ionian islands spent long periods under Venetian or other European rule. That let them absorb Europe's radical artistic changes much better.

The Cretan School of icon painting, also known as Post-Byzantine art, flourished while Crete was under Venetian rule. It became the central force in Greek painting during the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries. Its artists developed a style shaped by both Eastern and Western artistic traditions.

In 1751 James "Athenian" Stuart and Nicholas Revett led an expedition to Greece funded by the Society of Dilettanti. Their findings, published in 1762 as the first volume of The Antiquities of Athens, began serious archaeological inquiry into ancient Greek architecture.

The Cretan school of icon painting flourished under Venetian rule and became the central force in Greek painting in the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries. Its artists blended Eastern and Western traditions, and its most famous product was El Greco.

El Greco was the most famous product of the Cretan School. He was the most successful of the many artists who tried to build a career in Western Europe. In his later career he also left the Byzantine style farthest behind him.

After Crete fell to the Ottomans in 1669, the Heptanese School succeeded the Cretan School as the leading school of Greek post-Byzantine painting. Like its predecessor, it combined Byzantine traditions with increasing Western European influence.

The Heptanese School, whose name means "the School of the seven islands", was based in the Ionian Islands. These islands were not part of Ottoman Greece from the middle of the 17th century until the middle of the 19th. The school also saw the first significant depiction of secular subjects in Greek painting.

Artists from the Ionian islands played an important and often pioneering role in the 18th century. They exploited the conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque ateliers, carrying those advances into Greek painting.

Visiting Ottoman Greece was difficult and dangerous business before the period of stagnation that began with the Great Turkish War. Few tourists visited Athens in the first half of the 18th century, and none made any significant study of its architectural ruins. Despite the prestige of ancient Greece among Europe's educated elite, most people had minimal direct knowledge of it, and the monuments of Greek antiquity were known chiefly from Pausanias and other literary sources.

Julien-David Le Roy's Ruines des plus beaux monuments de la Grèce, published in 1758, was among the first accurate surveys of ancient Greek architecture. Along with Stuart and Revett's work, it gave Europeans reliable knowledge of Greek buildings for the first time.
tags: Ruines des plus beaux monuments de la Grèce

war.text: By the early 16th century the Ottomans had conquered nearly the whole of the Balkans and reached central Europe. Only a few small territories, such as Montenegro and the trading hub of Ragusa, kept any autonomy or independence.
The Ottomans took the last Venetian and Genoese holdings in Greece one by one. Rhodes fell in 1522 and Cyprus in 1571, while the Venetians held on to Crete until 1670.
The Greek revolts of the 18th century were unsuccessful, yet they were far larger than the revolts of earlier centuries. They laid the foundation for the national revolution that came later.

The Orlov Revolt of the 1770s was sponsored by Russia and had limited success before the Ottomans crushed it. After the uprising was suppressed, Muslim Albanians ravaged many regions of mainland Greece.
The Maniots continually resisted Ottoman rule and defeated several Ottoman incursions into their region. The most famous of these was the invasion of 1770.

In 1711 Peter the Great launched his Pruth River Campaign. He appealed to Orthodox Christians to join the Russians and rise against the Turks to fight for "faith and homeland", which set a precedent for the Greeks.

Russian agents incited an independence movement in Peloponnesus (Morea) in 1769. This came during the Russo-Turkish wars of Catherine II, which made the Greeks consider their emancipation with the aid of Russia.
During the Second Russo-Turkish War, the Greek community of Trieste financed a small fleet under Lambros Katsonis. It proved a nuisance for the Ottoman navy.

During the Second Russo-Turkish War, the klephts and armatoloi, guerilla fighters in mountainous areas, rose once again. Lambros Katsonis and his Greek flotilla assisted the Russian fleet in the war of 1788–1792.

literature.text: The Cretan Renaissance poem Erotokritos is called the masterpiece of the early period of modern Greek literature. It is a verse romance written around 1600 by Vitsentzos Kornaros, who lived from 1553 to 1613.

Under Venetian rule, Crete flourished in the late 16th and early 17th centuries and produced two of the most important Greek texts. These were Erofili (ca. 1595) by Georgios Chortatzis and Erotokritos (ca. 1600) by Vitsentzos Kornaros. Erofili is a violent tragedy about the condemned love between Erofili, daughter of the Egyptian king Philogonos, and the youth Panaretos.

The heyday of Cretan Renaissance literature is placed between 1590 and the Ottoman conquest of Crete in 1669. Almost all the works of this period are dramas. The two most prominent figures were Georgios Chortatzis and Vitsentzos Kornaros.

During the Cretan Renaissance in the 16th and early 17th centuries, a flourishing vernacular literature existed in the Cretan dialect, based on Italian literary influences. Its best-known specimen today is the verse romance Erotokritos, by Vitsentzos Kornaros (1553-1614).

Rigas Feraios wrote a battle-hymn, the Thourios, in 1797. In it he declared that it is finer to live one hour as a free man than forty years as a slave and prisoner. He urged Greeks and other Balkan peoples to leave Ottoman-occupied towns for the mountains, where they could find freedom and fight.
Another major voice of Cretan literature was Georgios Chortatzis, whose best-known work was Erofili. He also wrote the plays Panoria and Katsourbos, while Kornaros wrote The Sacrifice of Abraham.

Erotokritos is a long romantic poem of chivalry, lyric in character and didactic in purpose, written by Vitsentzos Kornaros, a hellenized Venetian of the 16th century. It draws on themes and ideas from the folk poetry of the time. In the story of Erotokritos and Arethusa, the poet glorifies love and friendship, chivalric courage, constancy, and self-sacrifice.
Kornaros is also believed by some to be the author of The Sacrifice of Abraham (1635), a religious drama inspired by the Old Testament episode. It is considered a landmark of Cretan theatre.
After 1669, many Cretans fled to the Ionian islands, transplanting the rich Cretan theatrical tradition there. The tragedy Zenon, played in 1683, was written by an anonymous Cretan playwright.

In the 18th and early 19th centuries, the Ionian Islands, then also under Italian rule, became a centre of literary production in Demotic Greek. The best-known writer of that period was the poet Dionysios Solomos (1789-1857), who wrote the Greek national anthem (Hymn to Liberty).

Besides Erotokritos, the only non-drama text of the Cretan Renaissance period is Voskopoula (ca. 1600), a short narrative poem of unknown author. Other surviving plays include the comedy Fortounatos (ca. 1662) by Markos Antonios Foskolos and the dramatic King Rodolinos (1647) by Andreas Troilos.

Petros Katsaitis' tragedies Ifigenia (1720) and Thyestes (1721), and Savoyas Soumerlis' satirical Comedy of the Pseudo-Doctors (1745), were evidently modelled after Cretan plays. They also show the influence of late Renaissance tragedy, commedia dell'arte, and Italian theatre in general.

The most important poem of the early 18th century is Flowers of Piety (1708), a miscellany edited by boarding students at the Flanginian College in Venice. Ecclesiastical rhetoric also made up a significant part of the intellectual output of the time.

Adamantios Korais, a leading figure of the Diafotismos, favoured a more conservative form of the Greek language, closer to the ancient. His linguistic views later became the target of a lampoon called Korakistika.

Theatrical activity on the Aegean islands continued in the first decades of the 18th century. Examples include the anonymous David, written in frankochiotika, and the Tragedy of St. Demetrius, performed in 1723 on Naxos.

In the Ottoman-held Balkans, the town of Vardar Yenicesi was unusual because Persian was widely spoken there. The 16th-century Ottoman Aşık Çelebi (died 1572), who hailed from Prizren, called the city a "hotbed of Persian", as it became the site of a flourishing Persianate linguistic and literary culture.

science.text: Roger Joseph Boscovich was born in 1711 in Dubrovnik, in the Republic of Ragusa. He was a physicist, astronomer, mathematician, Jesuit priest and polymath. He produced a precursor of atomic theory and made many contributions to astronomy.

Eugenios Voulgaris, born on Corfu in 1716, was a Greek Orthodox cleric who was also a mathematician, astronomer and physicist. He wrote about nearly every discipline, including astronomy, mathematics and the tides. He was a leading contributor to the Modern Greek Enlightenment.

Athanasios Psalidas ran the Maroutsaia School in Ioannina, later renamed Kaplaneios, for 25 years. He added natural sciences, history, geography and economics to its curriculum. Locals as well as students came to watch his lessons.

In 1753 Boscovich discovered the absence of an atmosphere on the Moon. He also devised the first geometric procedure for determining the equator of a rotating planet from three observations of a surface feature.

Psalidas brought educational equipment and special instruments to Ioannina to teach astronomy. He also performed a number of chemical and physical experiments at the school, and opened its library to the public.

From 1753 to 1759 Voulgaris directed the Athonite Academy at Vatopedi Monastery, where he taught philosophy and mathematics. His eagerness to share new Enlightenment ideas provoked a negative reaction among some Orthodox leaders on Mount Athos. He was forced to leave the school at the beginning of 1759.
Boscovich agreed to join a Portuguese expedition to survey Brazil and measure a degree of latitude. The Pope persuaded him to stay in Italy and carry out a similar task there instead.
The Royal Society of London invited Boscovich to go to California to observe the 1769 transit of Venus. The Spanish government's recent decree expelling Jesuits from its dominions prevented the trip.

Voulgaris studied theology, philosophy, European languages and natural sciences at the University of Padua after becoming a monk. In 1788 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, by which time he was living in Russia.
Voulgaris was one of the students of Methodios Anthrakites. He translated many important foreign-language academic documents into Greek, and also translated many texts from Latin into French.

A French translation of Boscovich's arc-measurement account appeared in 1770. It included material first published in 1760 on an objective way to fit a model to many observations. An unconstrained variant is now known as the L1-norm, or Least absolute deviations procedure, a robust alternative to Least Squares.

politics.text: Suleiman the Magnificent captured Belgrade in 1521. After his victory at the Battle of Mohács in 1526, he established Ottoman rule in the territory of present-day Hungary and other Central European territories.
Transylvania, Wallachia and, intermittently, Moldavia became tributary principalities of the Ottoman Empire. Under Suleiman the Magnificent, the empire became a global power in the 16th century.

In the 18th century Catherine the Great advanced the "Greek Plan". It would have driven the Ottomans out of Europe and liberated the Christians in the Balkans. Two new states would replace them: a "Kingdom of Dacia" in the north and a restored Byzantine Empire in the south.

Serbia's early modern period ran from the Ottoman conquest in the second half of the 15th century to the start of the Serbian Revolution in 1804. It included periods of Ottoman and Habsburg rule in various parts of Serbia, and several Habsburg–Ottoman wars were fought on Serbian territory.

Manuel Palaiologos, second son of Thomas Palaiologos, surprised people in Western Europe by returning to Constantinople and living out his life under Ottoman rule. His son Andreas died during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, and his death marks the end of the confidently verifiable imperial Palaiologos line.

The Italian Gonzaga family claimed a Palaiologos inheritance through the Palaeologus-Montferrat family. Their claims peaked under Vincenzo II Gonzaga and Charles I Gonzaga, who both aspired to lead crusades against the Ottomans and claim the Byzantine throne.

philosophy.text: In the 18th century, the Diafotismos movement carried the ideas and values of the European Enlightenment into the Greek world. It was ideological, philological, linguistic and philosophical, and its most notable figures were Adamantios Korais and Rigas Feraios.

For about two hundred years, Greek schools taught a philosophy created by Theophilos Corydalleus, a Neo-Aristotelian who believed Aristotelian thought should be kept free of Platonic influence. Known as Korydalism, it became the philosophical education of southeastern Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries. At one point its influence was so strong that the system disallowed new philosophical thought.

The Modern Greek Enlightenment was the Greek expression of the Age of Enlightenment, an intellectual and philosophical movement within the Greek community. Many Greeks were then dispersed across the Ottoman Empire, the Ionian Islands, Venice and other parts of Italy. Italy was the educational center for the Greek community.

Iosipos Moisiodax published The Apology in 1780, the first essay of Neohellenic literature. It proposed a "sound philosophy", meaning Western natural philosophy, as opposed to Corydalean Neo-Aristotelianism. He admired Descartes, Galilei, Christian Wolff, John Locke and above all Isaac Newton.

Methodios Anthrakites was a central figure in the break from Korydalism, fighting to bring updated European philosophical thought into Greek education. Church fathers persecuted him in Constantinople. A debate among Greek scholars followed in the later 18th century about changing education.

Cyril Lucaris, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, is said to have tried to reform the Eastern Orthodox Church along Calvinist lines. He sent many young Greek theologians to universities in Switzerland, the northern Netherlands and England. In 1629 he published his famous Confessio, which started a controversy in the Eastern Church.

Cyril Lucaris was condemned and later acquitted. The Council of Constantinople in 1638 anathematised him and the Eastern Confession of the Christian Faith. That same year, on 27 June 1638, Sultan Murad IV had him strangled by the Janissaries aboard a ship in the Bosporus, and his body was thrown into the sea, though it was recovered and buried in Nicomedia. The Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 condemned the Calvinistic doctrines but completely acquitted Cyril, saying he was cursed only because he had not written a rebuttal to the essay attributed to him.

Moisiodax's philosophy teaching in Iași, influenced by John Locke, brought him into conflict with the exponents of traditional order and led to his resignation in 1766. That year he fell sick, possibly of tuberculosis, retired from the professorship and went to Wallachia, where he spent the next 10 years. Once he had recovered, he returned to Iași as director of the Academy, but after only several months he was forced to resign again because of the boyars' opposition to his way of teaching. He also faced criticism and threats of violence for spreading his ideas.

Theophilos Corydalleus was criticized and suspected of atheism, and he and Cyril Lucaris were both accused of following the new Calvinist faith. Even so, Corydalleus was never seriously persecuted and continued to teach. His students included Patriarch Nectarius of Jerusalem and Meletios Syrigos.

The Greek language question began at the end of the 18th century. Eugenios Voulgaris proposed that modern Greek be archaised to resemble Ancient Greek. His students Iosipos Moisiodax and Dimitrios Katartzis preferred the contemporary vernacular, Dimotiki, and the debate became crucial to choosing the official language of the modern Greek state.

Nicholas Mavrocordatos, Prince of Wallachia, was influenced by the Age of Enlightenment. He wrote an original work entitled Peri kathekonton, or Liber de Officiis, published in Bucharest in 1719. He also wrote the first Greek novel, Philotheou Parerga, or The Leisures of Philotheos.

culture.text: Under the Ottoman millet arrangement, Orthodox Christians were placed in the Rum Millet, or "Roman nation", and enjoyed a certain autonomy. Greeks, Bulgarians, Albanians, Serbs and others were counted as one community, even though their languages and ethnicity differed.

Klephtic songs were ballads that grew up among the mountain bandits of Greece under Ottoman rule. They told of the achievements and death of a single klepht, or of the life of the klephts as a group, and remain especially popular in Epirus and the Peloponnese.

The devshirme was the Ottoman practice of forcibly taking boys aged 7 to 20 from Balkan Christian families, relocating them to Istanbul, and converting, circumcising and raising them as Muslims to serve as soldiers and officials. A firman of 1601 ordered officials to kill any parent who resisted, and a parent who refused was hanged from his door-sill; children who fled led the Turks to arrest and torture their parents to death. The system effectively stopped by 1648, but it left a mark on family life: in 1646 the Roman Catholic bishop of Chios wrote to ask the Catholic Greek Gymnasion of Rome to accept Paulos Omeros, a 12-year-old boy, to save him from the devshirme.

Phanariots were wealthy Greek families of the Phanar quarter of Constantinople, who were mostly patrons of Greek culture, education and printing. They founded academies that drew teachers and pupils from across the Orthodox world and kept up with intellectual trends in Habsburg Europe.
In 1539 the Greeks of Venice were permitted to begin building their own church, San Giorgio dei Greci. It still stands in the centre of Venice on the Rio dei Greci.

Janissaries were forbidden to marry until retirement, typically in their 40s, and could not engage in trade. By the 17th century the rules relaxed, and civilians bought their way into the corps to gain the better social and economic standing it offered.

After Constantinople fell, Hagia Sophia and the Parthenon, Christian churches for nearly a millennium, were converted into mosques. The number of churches and monasteries was greatly reduced to make room for new mosques, and the majority of churches became mosques during Ottoman rule, many by the close of the 16th century, like the Chora Church. Many churches were also destroyed, and only some were given maintenance, while new ones were built even more rarely.
culture.source_title: History of the Eastern Orthodox Church under the Ottoman Empire

culture.text: Kolokotronis, later a leader of the Greek War of Independence, was born in 1770 into a clan of fighters. His father, Konstantinos Kolokotronis, a former Armatoloi captain who had joined the Orlov Revolt, was killed in 1780 in an engagement with Ottoman troops, along with two of his brothers, George and Apostolis. Afterwards Mitros Petrovas took the boy in and taught him his first lessons about fighting; Kolokotronis always called him "uncle". Late in life he learned to write in order to complete his memoirs.

Messina is home to a small Greek-speaking minority. Its ancestors arrived from the Peloponnese between 1533 and 1534, fleeing the expansion of the Ottoman Empire, and the community was officially recognised only in 2012.

The Bektashi Order became the official religious and spiritual institution of the Janissaries in the 15th century. It served as a kind of chaplaincy for the sultan's elite household troops, who followed the teachings of the saint Haji Bektash Veli.

Phanariot rulers also shaped daily life in the Danubian principalities. As prince of Wallachia in 1746 and of Moldavia in 1749, Constantine Mavrocordatos abolished serfdom, and Alexander Ypsilantis of Wallachia (reigned 1774-1782) launched wide administrative and legal reforms.

In the 18th century the Rum millet set its own laws, collected its own taxes, and increasingly built its own schools, churches and hospitals. This was a way of religious community life that effectively moved the Christian population outside the Ottoman political system.
culture.source_title: History of the Eastern Orthodox Church under the Ottoman Empire

culture.text: Around 1550 the Greek poet Ioannes Axayiolis wrote a poem appealing to Emperor Charles V to liberate the Christians from the Turks, and it refers to the devshirme. In 1585 the Tübingen manuscript, given to Martin Crusius, recorded the grief of Christian parents over the Janissaries: mothers scratching out their cheeks, fathers beating their breasts with stones, and mothers saying it would have been better to see their children dead and buried in their church than taken alive to become Turks and abjure their faith.
